item.title: Deep dive: Giving evidence in a Court of Protection serious medical treatment hearing
item.description:
A practical medicolegal episode (England and Wales) for an ICU consultant about to give oral evidence in a contested best-interests case about escalation. Who is in the room (Trust counsel, Official Solicitor for P, family, sometimes an independent expert, Tier 3 judge, hybrid attendance, transparency orders); how the judge weighs P's wishes, feelings, values and beliefs under s.4 (Aintree, Wye Valley NHS Trust v B, Briggs v Briggs) and why "futility" language lands badly; the clinician's duty to the court; fact versus opinion; making benefits and burdens concrete; cross-examination lines of attack with a worked weak and better answer; and practical points. General discussion only, not legal advice, and no real case details.

Things to remember walking in

  • Your duty is to the court, not the Trust.
  • The question is what is best for this person, with their values and wishes carrying real weight; not whether treatment is "futile".
  • Make benefits and burdens concrete and be honest about uncertainty.
  • In cross-examination concede true facts quickly and hold reasoned conclusions.
  • Keep fact, opinion and matters outside your expertise separate.
  • Short answers, address the judge, correct your statement at the start, and "I don't know" is acceptable.

item.title: Deep dive: Clotting tests: what they measure and how to use them
item.description:
What PT, APTT, Clauss fibrinogen, thrombin time, platelet count and D-dimer measure, set against the cell-based model of haemostasis (Hoffman and Monroe 2001). Standard tests predict procedural bleeding poorly (Segal and Dzik 2005), plasma often fails to correct a mildly raised INR (Holland and Brooks 2006) and rebalanced haemostasis in cirrhosis makes the INR misleading. DOAC presence needs drug-calibrated anti-Xa or thrombin time, not PT and APTT; isolated prolonged APTT work-up is covered. Viscoelastic testing: Cochrane 2026 (35 RCTs, very low certainty), ITACTIC (neutral), OBS2, Welsh PPH data, NICE DG13/HTG348. Neuraxial: the 2013 Association, OAA and RA-UK guidance is still current (no 2025 replacement was found), with Shah 2025 as cross-check.

Take-home points

  • PT, APTT and INR were not built to predict bleeding; do not treat the number.
  • Plasma is a poor way to correct an INR, and a long INR in liver disease is not a coagulopathy needing correction.
  • To exclude a DOAC use anti-Xa or thrombin time, never PT and APTT.
  • In bleeding, fibrinogen is the test that matters, especially in obstetrics; viscoelastic evidence is thin outside cardiac surgery.
  • For neuraxial blocks use the 2013 guideline, cross-checked against Shah 2025; no new guideline exists.

item.title: Deep dive: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing before surgery
item.description:
Consultant-level review of preoperative CPET: V-slope anaerobic threshold physiology, effort-dependence and reader variability, and where the quoted thresholds come from (Older 1993 AT 11 in elderly abdominal surgery; Wilson 2010 VE/VCO2 34 in 847 colorectal patients with 18 deaths; lung resection peak VO2 10 and 20). Stubbs 2020 shows CPET rules out better than it rules in. The blinded METS study (Lancet 2018, 1401 patients) found peak VO2 predicted moderate or severe complications but not death or MI, AT predicted none, and DASI and NT-proBNP predicted other outcomes; subjective assessment was insensitive. Guidelines are quiet on CPET, and no trial shows CPET-guided care improves outcomes; prehabilitation evidence is moderate but not CPET-specific.

Take-home points

  • Know where thresholds come from: AT 11 is Older 1993, VE/VCO2 34 is Wilson 2010, both single-centre and not pass/fail lines.
  • In METS peak VO2 predicted complications, not death or MI; AT predicted nothing.
  • Subjective assessment misses most low-capacity patients; use DASI or a measured test.
  • Check effort and technical quality before trusting a value.
  • Use CPET to inform shared decisions and plan care; there is no trial evidence it improves outcomes.

item.title: Deep dive: Intravenous iron and preoperative anaemia
item.description:
Perioperative pitch on IV iron before surgery. Iron deficiency is diagnosed with ferritin and transferrin saturation, but definitions of functional deficiency are contested. PREVENTT (Lancet 2020, 487 patients, major open abdominal surgery) was neutral on death or transfusion (28 vs 29 per cent) with a modest haemoglobin rise; the lower readmission rate was a secondary outcome and hypothesis-generating. Its post hoc analysis found 82 per cent were iron deficient, with the haemoglobin gain concentrated in absolute deficiency. ITACS (BMJ 2026, 955 cardiac surgery patients) gave a one-day gain in days alive and at home (P 0.041) and less transfusion (61 vs 68 per cent). Network meta-analyses are indirect and conflicting on timing; critical care trials (IRONMAN, HEPCIDANE) do not support routine iron. Formulations, dosing from SmPCs, FCM hypophosphataemia and guideline status (NICE NG24 from 2015, BSH 2024) are discussed.

Take-home points

  • Check ferritin and transferrin saturation early before major elective surgery.
  • Absolute iron deficiency with roughly six weeks or less to surgery: IV iron is reasonable, supported in cardiac surgery by ITACS.
  • Expect a modest effect on haemoglobin and transfusion, not on mortality.
  • Ferric carboxymaltose causes hypophosphataemia, particularly with repeat doses (MHRA Drug Safety Update, 2020).
  • No routine iron in critical illness.

item.title: Deep dive: Ward round round-up: six common ICU admissions
item.description:
Post-VF arrest, day 5 to 7: TTM2 and the 2025 ERC-ESICM guideline favour active fever prevention (37.5 C or below, 36 to 72 h) over deep cooling, prognosis is multimodal (two or more indicators, at least 72 h, confounders excluded), and angiography without ST elevation can be delayed (COACT neutral, TOMAHAWK borderline). Acute limb ischaemia after revascularisation: ESVS 2020 supports heparin before revascularisation, clinical vigilance for post-reperfusion compartment syndrome with emergency four-compartment fasciotomy (not delayed beyond 6 h, NCEPOD 2025 says ideally within 2 h), and awareness of rhabdomyolysis-related renal injury; NICE CG147 covers chronic disease only. Spontaneous ICH: BP evidence is mixed (INTERACT2, ATACH-2, INTERACT3 bundle), guidelines favour early systolic below 140 while avoiding overshoot, reversal agents differ in evidence quality (PCC/vitamin K, andexanet with thrombotic signal in ANNEXA-I, idarucizumab), surgery benefit is limited to selected cases (ENRICH lobar), and VTE prevention relies on IPC with LMWH timing based on small trials and consensus. Hypercapnic COPD exacerbation: BTS/ICS 2016 starts NIV at pH below 7.35 with PCO2 above 6.5 kPa persisting after medical therapy; Cochrane (Osadnik 2017) shows lower mortality and intubation; HFNC is unproven as a replacement; NIV needs an agreed failure plan and ceiling, and stage 2 AKI needs a cause search and pharmacy dose review. Guillain-Barre syndrome: trend vital capacity, MIP, MEP and bulbar function (20/30/40 from a retrospective series); IVIG and plasma exchange are similar; a second IVIG dose (SID-GBS) did not help and caused more serious adverse events; eculizumab missed its primary endpoint; efgartigimod is not approved for GBS. Acute pancreatitis: moderate, reassessed fluids rather than aggressive (WATERFALL); early oral feeding rather than routine tube feeding (PYTHON); step-up drainage for infected necrosis (PANTER, TENSION) with postponed drainage not worse than immediate (POINTER); treat alcohol withdrawal and give thiamine.

Take-home points

  • After VF arrest the 2025 guidance is fever prevention, not deep hypothermia; TTM2 showed 50 vs 48 per cent death at 6 months.
  • Do not prognosticate on a single test or before 72 h with sedation confounders; two or more concordant indicators are required, otherwise keep observing.
  • Without ST elevation, angiography can be delayed unless occlusion is likely.
  • After limb revascularisation examine the compartments, track potassium, CK, creatinine and urine output; do not delay fasciotomy once compartment syndrome is diagnosed.
  • Be explicit about why a patient is anticoagulated and for how long; the guideline gives no fixed post-operative heparin duration.
  • In ICH, set and document a systolic target (about 140), avoid overshoot below about 110 to 130, reverse promptly according to the agent, and weigh andexanet's thrombotic risk.
  • Ask neurosurgery explicitly; evidence for surgery is strongest for selected lobar bleeds with minimally invasive techniques (ENRICH), neutral elsewhere.
  • Start intermittent pneumatic compression on admission; LMWH from about 24 to 48 hours after stable imaging is consensus-level.
  • Check the gas before and after starting or changing NIV, and decide and document whether NIV is the ceiling.
  • Stage 2 AKI: KDIGO creatinine 2.0 to 2.9 times baseline or urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 12 hours; review nephrotoxins and renal dosing with pharmacy.
  • GBS: trend FVC, pressures and bulbar function; do not give a routine second IVIG dose; use prognostic scores as estimates only.
  • Pancreatitis: moderate goal-directed fluids with daily overload checks; early oral feeding; antibiotics for suspected infection not prophylaxis; postpone drainage of infected necrosis if stable; treat alcohol withdrawal and give parenteral thiamine.

item.title: Deep dive: Major burns resuscitation and inhalation injury
item.description:
Major burns resuscitation and inhalation injury. ABA 2024 guideline (adults with burns of 20 percent TBSA or more, first 48 hours) recommends starting at 2 mL/kg/%TBSA rather than Parkland's 4, titrating to urine output of 0.5 mL/kg/h, considering albumin, and selectively monitoring intra-abdominal pressure; it makes no recommendation on vitamin C, FFP, early CRRT or vasopressors. ABRUPT (2023) was observational and confounded; ABRUPT2 (2026) randomised 99 patients before stopping early and showed albumin reduced 24 and 48 hour fluid with no mortality, healing or AKI difference but heavy crossover. Hydroxocobalamin evidence (Borron 2007, Fortin 2006) is uncontrolled. Nebulised heparin has a 2020 meta-analysis of nine mostly small trials (mortality RR 0.75), but HEPBURN stopped after 13 patients with no efficacy analysis. Propranolol and oxandrolone have meta-analytic support for metabolic outcomes but oxandrolone shows no mortality benefit and more transaminase rises. Revised Baux score = age + %TBSA + 17 if inhalation injury (Osler 2010). Exact wording of the UK National Burn Care Referral Guidance could not be verified; a NHS burns unit summary is cited instead.

Take-home points

  • Start burn shock resuscitation at 2 mL/kg per percent TBSA and titrate to about 0.5 mL/kg/h urine output, avoiding fluid creep.
  • Albumin reduces fluid volume (ABRUPT2, small, stopped early, heavy crossover) but survival benefit is unproven.
  • Secure the airway early when inhalation injury is suspected; treat CO and possible cyanide poisoning clinically, knowing hydroxocobalamin evidence is uncontrolled.
  • Do not rely on nebulised heparin (HEPBURN stopped early); watch for limb, chest and abdominal compartment syndromes.
  • Phone the burns service early and use the revised Baux score to frame honest proportionality conversations.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe accidental hypothermia and heat stroke
item.description:
Swiss staging, rescue collapse, and ECLS rewarming in hypothermic cardiac arrest, with the HOPE score (derivation and validations, a 2025 Swiss two-centre series, the 2024 ELSO-criteria cohort, the new HELP score) and ERC 2025 guidance; then heat stroke: exertional versus classic, SCCM 2025 guideline favouring active cooling and cold or ice-water immersion, organ failure including rhabdomyolysis, DIC and liver, UK heat mortality context, outcomes and grey zones.

Take-home points

  • Handle stage three hypothermia gently and route stage three or four patients to an ECPR centre.
  • Do not rely on potassium alone; use HOPE as a decision aid, not a veto.
  • Age, asystole or unwitnessed arrest alone should not stop ECLS rewarming.
  • In heat stroke cool first with the fastest available method and avoid antipyretics.
  • Keep checking liver, clotting and CK for days.

item.title: Deep dive: Serotonin syndrome, NMS and malignant hyperthermia
item.description:
Telling the hyperthermic, rigid ICU patient apart. Hunter criteria (clonus-led, derived in overdose cohorts, poorly validated in polypharmacy ICU patients), the Delphi consensus NMS criteria (not yet validated for clinical use), and the Association of Anaesthetists 2020 MH guideline (trigger removal, dantrolene 2 to 3 mg/kg then 1 mg/kg every 5 minutes to ETCO2 below 6 kPa and core temperature below 38.5, reappraise at 10 mg/kg, 24 hours of HDU/ICU, direct referral to the Leeds MH Investigation Unit). Severe serotonin toxicity is managed by early resuscitation, benzodiazepines, intubation, paralysis and cooling; cyproheptadine and other antagonists lack conclusive evidence. In NMS, failure to stop the antipsychotic predicts death in case-report data. ICU drug interactions: linezolid, methylene blue, fentanyl, ondansetron, mostly case-based evidence.

Take-home points

  • Examine for clonus and tone and review the last three days of drugs, including missed dopaminergic doses.
  • Stop the culprit and cool; intubate and paralyse early if rigid and above 38.5 rather than wait for the label.
  • Volatile on board with rising ETCO2 and heat: dantrolene 2 to 3 mg/kg, then refer to the Leeds MH Unit.
  • Cyproheptadine and bromocriptine/dantrolene in NMS rest on case reports; do not let them delay supportive care.
  • Check linezolid and methylene blue against the chart before starting either.

item.title: Deep dive: Necrotising soft tissue infections
item.description:
Recognition is clinical: LRINEC has poor sensitivity (about 68 percent at six or more) and should not rule out NSTI. Early surgical debridement is the one intervention with a consistent mortality signal (observational meta-analysis: odds ratio 0.43 for surgery within six hours). Clindamycin or linezolid for toxin suppression is mechanistically plausible but untested in randomised trials. INSTINCT (100 patients, all-cause NSTI) found no benefit of IVIG; the streptococcal toxic shock evidence is a 21-patient terminated trial plus a null propensity-matched cohort. Hyperbaric oxygen remains unproven, with observational data heavily confounded. iGAS is notifiable and UKHSA contact guidance was updated in September 2025. Fournier's gangrene follows the same surgical principles.

Take-home points

  • LRINEC cannot rule out NSTI; high suspicion plus surgical exploration is the diagnosis.
  • Debridement within hours is the only intervention with a consistent mortality signal; do not let imaging or adjuncts delay theatre.
  • Clindamycin or linezolid is reasonable with streptococcal or toxic shock features but is not trial-proven.
  • IVIG showed no benefit in all-comer NSTI (INSTINCT); consider it for streptococcal toxic shock only. Hyperbaric oxygen is unproven and never worth delaying care.
  • Notify iGAS early and check current UKHSA contact guidance.

item.title: Deep dive: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage and pulmonary-renal syndromes
item.description:
Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage in pulmonary-renal syndromes: causes (A N C A vasculitis, anti G B M, lupus, post-transplant), serology over lavage, pulse steroids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and the plasma exchange debate after PEXIVAS (negative overall, only about nine percent severe haemorrhage). KDIGO 2024 and BSR 2025 differ on exchange for hypoxaemic haemorrhage with preserved kidney function. ADVOCATE (avacopan) was retracted by NEJM on 29 June 2026; the reason was taken from press reports and should be checked against the notice. ICU ventilation and ECMO advice rests on observational data and expert opinion.

Take-home points

  • Suspect haemorrhage in unexplained bilateral shadowing with anaemia and dip the urine.
  • Send A N C A and anti G B M urgently and involve renal and rheumatology before results.
  • After excluding infection, pulse methylprednisolone plus rituximab or cyclophosphamide.
  • Plasma exchange is standard for anti G B M, discretionary otherwise; KDIGO and BSR disagree for isolated hypoxaemic haemorrhage.
  • Consider early ECMO referral as a bridge (observational evidence only); treat avacopan evidence cautiously after the ADVOCATE retraction.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute severe asthma
item.description:
Acute severe asthma: the November 2024 BTS/NICE/SIGN joint guideline covers chronic asthma only; acute attack management remains in BTS/SIGN 158 (2019), with a standalone revalidation planned. Evidence for adjuncts is thin: IV magnesium reduces admissions in Cochrane (2014) but 3Mg (1109 adults, 2013) was negative and excluded life-threatening cases; nebulised magnesium in MAGNETIC (508 children) gave a statistically but not clinically significant benefit; heliox has no overall benefit (Cochrane 2006, 10 trials, 544 patients); ketamine has one paediatric RCT (68 children) and no adult RCT found; NIV is promising but controversial. Ventilation strategy (low rate, long expiratory time, permissive hypercapnia) is physiology and consensus. ELSO registry data (Yeo 2017, 272 patients) show 83.5 percent survival to discharge with frequent complications. NRAD (2014, 195 deaths) found at least one avoidable factor in 67 percent.

Take-home points

  • The 2024 joint guideline does not cover acute attacks; use BTS/SIGN 158 (2019) until the revalidated version appears.
  • Normal or rising PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic means involve ICU early.
  • IV magnesium 1.2 to 2 g for life-threatening features is guideline-supported, but trial evidence excluded the sickest patients.
  • If intubating, plan settings first: low rate, long expiratory time, tolerate hypercapnia, know to disconnect the circuit for hyperinflation collapse.
  • Discuss ECMO early with the centre, and make follow-up after discharge happen (NRAD).

item.title: Deep dive: Pulmonary hypertension in the ICU
item.description:
Decompensated pulmonary arterial hypertension in ICU: a chronic, afterload-stressed right ventricle with little reserve. Evidence is almost entirely observational cohorts, physiology and expert review. A 2025 meta-analysis of 25 observational studies (1,249 patients) found ICU mortality 29 percent, hospital mortality 38 percent, ECMO 45 percent, with no improvement over twenty years. Practical consensus: early contact with the specialist PH centre, never interrupt prostanoids, treat triggers, diurese rather than fluid load if overloaded, noradrenaline with early vasopressin, cautious inotropes, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, avoid intubation or plan it meticulously, and consider early VA ECMO as bridge with goals of care agreed first.

Take-home points

  • Phone the specialist pulmonary hypertension centre early.

item.title: Deep dive: Anaphylaxis and refractory anaphylaxis
item.description:
Anaphylaxis has almost no randomised evidence; UK practice rests on the Resuscitation Council UK 2021 guideline (GRADE-ADOLOPMENT, mostly very low certainty evidence) and, in anaesthesia, the NAP6 audit (266 grade 3 to 5 reactions, incidence about 1 in 10,000 anaesthetics, 10 deaths, antibiotics and neuromuscular blockers the commonest culprits, chlorhexidine and Patent Blue delayed in onset). Refractory anaphylaxis (no improvement after two IM adrenaline doses) is treated with fluids, an IV adrenaline infusion (1 mg in 100 mL, 0.5 mL/kg/h), a second vasopressor and glucagon in beta-blocked patients, all on low-grade evidence. Antihistamines and steroids are not routine. Biphasic reactions occur in about 4 to 5 per cent in observational data, and RCUK now advises risk-stratified observation of 2, 6 or 12 hours, which NICE NG258 adopted in May 2026. Serial timed tryptase and allergy clinic referral are recommended for all.

Take-home points

  • Give IM adrenaline early and repeat at 5 minutes; do not let antihistamines or steroids delay it.
  • Two ineffective IM doses means refractory: fluids, adrenaline infusion, expert help, and compressions in arrest even if the trace looks flat.
  • In beta-blocked patients with adrenaline-resistant shock consider glucagon, but the evidence is case reports; a second vasopressor has no human comparative data.
  • Take timed tryptase (early, 1 to 2 hours, and a baseline at least 24 hours later) and record drug timings.
  • Refer every perioperative anaphylaxis to an allergy clinic, and set observation length by risk rather than habit.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute aortic dissection
item.description:
Acute aortic dissection deep dive for an ICU consultant. Covers HSIB 2020 findings on delayed recognition (incidence about 4.5 per 100,000, delay in 16 to 40 percent, recommendations on triage and a national RCEM/RCR process), ADD-RS plus D-dimer (ADvISED, Circulation 2018) and the ESC 2024 class I algorithm, anti-impulse therapy with a real disagreement between ESC 2024 (SBP under 120, HR 60 or less) and the ACC/AHA 2022 guideline as summarised by the ACC (SBP under 120, HR 60 to 80), type A surgery and the limits of the evidence on who is turned down, malperfusion syndromes, complicated versus uncomplicated type B and the INSTEAD, INSTEAD-XL and ADSORB trials (remodelling benefit, no proven survival benefit in randomised data), IMPROVE-AD ongoing, post-operative ICU care and spinal protection (CSF drain RCT is from elective TAAA repair, not dissection), and IRAD outcome trends.

Take-home points

  • Score every suspected case with ADD-RS: two or more goes straight to CT from neck to pelvis; D-dimer only helps in the low-score group and is not a rule-out on gestalt alone.
  • Start IV beta blocker first (labetalol or esmolol), then vasodilator, aim systolic under 120; agree the heart rate target locally because ESC says 60 or less and ACC/AHA says 60 to 80, and hold a higher MAP if spinal or brain ischaemia.
  • Type A is immediate surgery; age alone is not an exclusion in the ESC text, and the decision about shock, malperfusion or coma is a team judgement.
  • After surgery, look early for malperfusion and treat spinal cord perfusion pressure as its own question; CSF drain evidence comes from elective thoracoabdominal repair.
  • For uncomplicated type B, randomised data show remodelling but not proven survival benefit; discuss with the aortic team and watch for IMPROVE-AD.

item.title: Deep dive: Sickle cell crisis and acute chest syndrome
item.description:
Acute chest syndrome (ACS) is the leading cause of death in sickle cell disease and often develops after admission with pain. Evidence for transfusion is almost entirely observational: the Cochrane review found one eligible randomised trial with ten participants, and the single exchange versus simple comparison (Turner 2009) was a small retrospective study showing no difference in length of stay. BSH 2016 guidance recommends early simple transfusion for mild disease and exchange for severe ACS, simple-transfusion failure, stroke or multi-organ failure, with consensus-level targets. NIV has one open-label randomised pilot with faster physiological gain but no day-three difference. NICE CG143 sets analgesia within 30 minutes and reassessment every 30 minutes; the APPG 2021 inquiry reports care failings and negative attitudes. NCEPOD 2008 full report could not be opened, so only qualitative secondary-sourced concerns were used. No sickle-specific HFNO evidence was verified.

Take-home points

  • Think ACS in any sickle patient with new chest pain, fever, respiratory signs or falling saturations (NICE: saturation 95% or below).
  • Involve haematology early and have matched blood (Rh, Kell, sickle negative, antibody history) available.
  • Exchange for severe ACS, failed simple transfusion, acute stroke or multi-organ failure; avoid overshooting Hb (about 100 g/L target in stroke exchange; simple transfusion target 100-110 g/L). HbS target after exchange is consensus (under 30-40 percent).
  • Treat pain fast but watch respiratory rate and sedation; use incentive spirometry and sit up.
  • Listen to the patient; delayed transfusion reactions and hyperhaemolysis need specialist input.

item.title: Deep dive: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
item.description:
DIC is a syndrome of systemic coagulation activation, suppressed fibrinolysis and endothelial injury, most often driven by sepsis; it runs from an early thrombotic phase to a late consumptive, bleeding phase. Randomised evidence for specific anticoagulants is negative or inconclusive (KyberSept antithrombin 2001, SCARLET thrombomodulin 2019; heparin meta-analysis inconclusive), with positive signals mostly from post hoc subgroups and Japanese observational data. UK guidance (BSH 2009, now old) is transfusion-conservative and consensus-based; Japanese 2024 guidelines recommend antithrombin and thrombomodulin (GRADE 1B) while Surviving Sepsis 2016 recommended against antithrombin. ISTH 2025 (consensus) introduces pre-DIC, early-phase and overt DIC, with SIC as the early-phase sepsis tool.

Take-home points

  • DIC marks severity: control the source first; score platelets, INR, fibrinogen and D-dimer daily and follow the trend.
  • Use SIC (score 4 or more) for early detection and the ISTH overt score (5 or more) for late disease.
  • Replace products for bleeding or procedures (BSH: platelets under 50 if bleeding/high risk; plasma if bleeding with prolonged PT/APTT; fibrinogen concentrate or cryoprecipitate if under 1 g/L despite plasma), not for numbers alone.
  • Antithrombin, thrombomodulin and therapeutic heparin remain unproven in randomised trials; heparin is a consensus option in thrombotic-predominant DIC.
  • Keep TTP/TMA and HIT on the differential; phone haematology early.

item.title: Deep dive: Neutropenic sepsis and the haematology patient on ICU
item.description:
UK guidance (NICE CG151, 2012) treats suspected neutropenic sepsis as an emergency: immediate empirical piperacillin with tazobactam monotherapy, no routine aminoglycoside or glycopeptide, no switching for persistent fever alone unless the patient deteriorates. The 2018 German AGIHO/iCHOP consensus guideline (written for haematologists and intensivists) allows meropenem or imipenem and an aminoglycoside in septic shock, suggests considering antifungals with fungal risk factors or cardiopulmonary instability, and advises against routine G-CSF. Cochrane reviews show no significant mortality benefit for G-CSF (2014) or for empirical over pre-emptive antifungals (2022), both low certainty. Observational data (Azoulay JCO 2013; ICM 2019 individual-data meta-analysis) show ICU survival in haematological malignancy has improved, though not in allogeneic transplant recipients; earlier ICU admission is associated with better survival. For respiratory failure, neither early NIV (IVNIctus, 2015) nor high-flow oxygen (HIGH, 2018) changed day-28 mortality; early bronchoscopy added no clear diagnostic yield over non-invasive testing (2010). A 2026 retrospective Dutch analysis suggests prognosis gains little certainty over two weeks of ICU, supporting early goal-setting and time-limited trials with haematology.

Take-home points

  • Suspected neutropenic sepsis is an emergency: broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately (NICE: pip-taz monotherapy), escalate on deterioration or local microbiology, not on persistent fever alone.
  • NICE and the German consensus differ on aminoglycosides (NICE avoid by default; German group: may consider in septic shock). Neither is backed by ICU RCTs.
  • No routine G-CSF; antifungal decisions are joint with haematology and microbiology (pre-emptive looks no worse than empirical, low-certainty evidence, haematology ward populations).
  • Do not decline ICU on diagnosis alone; survival has improved over time (observational) and earlier ICU admission is associated with better survival.
  • HFNO and NIV show no clear mortality difference; do not delay intubation if failing. Agree goals and a time-limited trial early with haematology.

item.title: Deep dive: Autoimmune encephalitis
item.description:
Autoimmune encephalitis for UK ICU and anaesthesia, centred on anti-NMDA receptor (NMDAR) encephalitis. Antibodies cause reversible loss of synaptic NMDARs in cultured neurons (Hughes 2010). The Graus 2016 consensus criteria allow a diagnosis of probable disease before the antibody result (rapid onset of at least four of six symptom groups, plus abnormal EEG or CSF pleocytosis/oligoclonal bands, plus exclusion of other causes). Observational data support early first-line immunotherapy (steroids, IVIG, plasma exchange), tumour removal and, if no improvement, second-line rituximab or cyclophosphamide: Titulaer 2013 (577 patients; 53 percent of treated, assessable patients improved within 4 weeks; second-line associated with better outcome, OR 2.69), and a 2021 individual-patient meta-analysis (1,550 published cases; ICU admission, extreme delta brush and no immunotherapy in the first 30 days associated with poor outcome; rituximab associated with fewer relapses). ICU admission predicts worse outcome but is a marker of severity; a 2022 single-centre retrospective Chinese cohort found 77 percent of ventilated patients had a good outcome, with slower recovery after prolonged ventilation. The NEOS score estimates 1-year outcome (3 percent poor at 0 to 1 points, 69 percent at 4 to 5). The only randomised trial found, ExTINGUISH (inebilizumab), is still recruiting and has no reported results; no UK ABN guideline was found, and the NHS England rituximab policy status should be checked locally. NORSE/FIRES guidance is a 2022 Delphi consensus built on case series, with no randomised trials. Evidence on LGI1/CASPR2 was not reviewed in depth.

Take-home points

  • Consider NMDAR encephalitis in a young patient with rapid psychiatric change, seizures, dyskinesias, falling consciousness and autonomic instability or hypoventilation. Send CSF (and serum) antibodies and an EEG.
  • Do not wait for the antibody: once infection is reasonably excluded, start steroids and IVIG or plasma exchange (observational evidence and expert consensus; earlier treatment predicted better outcome in Titulaer 2013).
  • Look for an ovarian teratoma and involve neurology early about second-line therapy (rituximab, cyclophosphamide) if there is no improvement.
  • ICU admission and prolonged ventilation predict slower or worse recovery in cohorts, but many ventilated patients do well and recovery can continue for months (up to 18 months in Titulaer). A long stay alone should not drive a ceiling-of-care decision; consider time-limited trials with neurology input and an honest probability-based discussion.
  • NORSE/FIRES is a presentation, not a diagnosis; look for autoimmune causes, and use the 2022 consensus as a guide, recognising it is expert opinion.

item.description:
PRES and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (RCVS) for UK ICU and anaesthesia. PRES: Mayo series (Fugate 2010, 113 patients; seizures about three quarters, hypertension 61 percent, cytotoxic drugs 19, sepsis 7, pre-eclampsia or eclampsia 6), the endothelial dysfunction versus autoregulatory breakthrough debate (Lancet Neurology 2015 and 2025 reviews; the 2025 review states randomised evidence is absent), the French severe-PRES ICU cohort (Legriel 2012, 70 patients, 16 percent died by day 90, longer time to control of the causative factor associated with poor outcome) and haemorrhage in PRES (Hefzy 2009, 15.2 percent of 151). RCVS: Ducros 2012 review, the Massachusetts and Cleveland series (139 patients; steroids trended towards worse outcome, not significant), the RCVS2 score (Rocha, Neurology 2019, single-centre derivation; later external check showed sensitivity 64 percent and specificity 94 percent for angiographic vasoconstriction), verapamil case-level systematic review, and a 2025 individual patient data analysis of RCVS with convexity subarachnoid haemorrhage (138 patients, 94 percent of those with follow-up had little or no disability). Eclampsia is the one setting with trial evidence (Magpie 2002; NICE NG133 magnesium regimen). Blood pressure targets (about 20 to 25 percent MAP fall over 1 to 2 hours), antiseizure duration and magnesium outside obstetrics are expert opinion. No UK guideline specific to PRES or RCVS was found.

Take-home points

  • Consider PRES in an ICU patient with new seizure, encephalopathy or visual disturbance and a trigger (hypertension, eclampsia, calcineurin inhibitor, chemotherapy, sepsis, renal failure). Consider RCVS in thunderclap headache, especially postpartum or on serotonergic or vasoactive drugs. RCVS can mimic subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • A normal early scan or angiogram does not exclude either; RCVS vasoconstriction peaks 2 to 3 weeks after onset and strokes can follow a normal first image (Ducros 2012). The RCVS2 score helps but was derived in a small single-centre cohort.
  • Remove the trigger early and lower blood pressure steadily. The 20 to 25 percent MAP reduction over 1 to 2 hours and MAP 105 to 125 target come from secondary expert summaries borrowed from hypertensive emergencies, not PRES trials.
  • Eclampsia: intravenous magnesium (NICE NG133 regimen: 4 g loading, then 1 g per hour, continued 24 hours after the last fit), not diazepam or phenytoin as an alternative; severe hypertension treated immediately with labetalol, oral nifedipine or intravenous hydralazine. Magnesium in non-obstetric PRES is unproven.
  • In RCVS, nimodipine or verapamil is common practice but unproven for preventing stroke or haemorrhage; be cautious with steroids (observational signal of harm, confounded) and avoid serotonergic drugs and vasoconstrictors.

item.title: Deep dive: Toxic alcohols: methanol and ethylene glycol
item.description:
Toxic alcohols (methanol and ethylene glycol) for UK ICU and anaesthesia: the metabolic basis of toxicity (formate and glycolate/oxalate via alcohol dehydrogenase), the limits of the osmolar and anion gaps (Vancouver retrospective study of 131 patients: gap of 10 sensitive but poorly specific; a 2004 review calling the gap's clinical utility hypothetical; pH the best mortality predictor in a pooled case-report review), point-of-care lactate artefact with ethylene glycol, empirical treatment, fomepizole versus ethanol (no randomised trials; 2013 systematic review of 897 patients inconclusive; two single-arm Brent studies), the 2002 AACT methanol guideline, EXTRIP criteria for methanol (2015) and ethylene glycol (2023, very low quality evidence throughout), thin evidence for folate, thiamine and pyridoxine, outbreak data (Czech 2012: 121 patients, 34 percent total mortality; 2019 outbreak consensus), long-term visual outcomes (40 percent of 50 survivors), and brief notes on isopropanol and diethylene glycol. TOXBASE is login-only, so UK NPIS content could not be verified directly; only a secondary UK source was found.

Take-home points

  • A normal osmolar gap does not exclude methanol or ethylene glycol, especially in late presenters, and a raised gap is not specific. Use it with the anion gap, pH and, where possible, a measured level.
  • A point-of-care lactate that is high while the laboratory lactate is normal, in a well-perfused patient, can point to ethylene glycol (case reports).
  • If suspicion is real and a level is hours away, treat empirically with an alcohol dehydrogenase blocker and call the poisons service. Fomepizole is generally preferred over ethanol, though no randomised comparison exists.
  • Know the EXTRIP dialysis triggers: coma, seizures, new visual deficit, severe acidosis (methanol pH 7.15 or below), high anion gap, renal injury, or high levels. These are consensus recommendations graded on low quality evidence.
  • Cofactors (folinic or folic acid for methanol; thiamine and pyridoxine for ethylene glycol) are cheap and reasonable but not proven. In an outbreak, prioritise antidote, triage dialysis, and ask for help early.

item.title: Deep dive: Alcoholic and euglycaemic ketoacidosis
item.description:
Alcoholic and euglycaemic ketoacidosis for UK ICU and anaesthesia: alcoholic ketoacidosis (AKA) from the Wrenn case series (74 patients, 1991), the unreliable urine ketone dipstick and the osmol gap trap (55 AKA patients, median osmol gap 27, 2024 poison centre study), a 2026 multicentre emergency department review (905 alcohol-related presentations, AKA in 11 to 26 percent depending on definition), and the thin evidence behind the thiamine-before-dextrose rule (2012 review of 19 papers, none above case-report level; 2025 US Veterans Affairs retrospective study, 120 encounters, no Wernicke's). SGLT2-inhibitor ketoacidosis: meta-analyses (Colacci 2022, seven trials, RR 2.46; Wang 2025, 22 trials, RR 2.32, not significant in heart failure trials), the 2016 MHRA Drug Safety Update, the 2016 ABCD position statement, JBDS 2023 management of DKA including the euglycaemic DKA section, the 2025 Association of Anaesthetists-led UK perioperative consensus (omit the day before and the day of surgery) against the FDA 3 to 4 day advice and the 2026 SPAQI consensus. There are no randomised trials of AKA treatment and no robust outcome data for perioperative SGLT2 ketoacidosis; one planned observational study (NCT06838507) is not yet recruiting.

Take-home points

  • Anion gap acidosis with a normal glucose: measure capillary or blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, not urine ketones (JBDS 2023), and keep AKA and SGLT2-inhibitor ketoacidosis both on the list.
  • AKA: fluids with dextrose, thiamine given promptly alongside it, and replacement of potassium, magnesium and phosphate. This is based on physiology, case series and consensus rather than trials. If glucose is genuinely high, consider DKA in a drinker.
  • Do not delay dextrose to give thiamine first; the evidence for that rule is case-report level. Give both together. A high osmol gap in AKA is common and should not by itself trigger fomepizole or dialysis without a toxic alcohol level.
  • SGLT2-inhibitor ketoacidosis is treated as DKA per JBDS 2023: 10 percent glucose at 125 ml per hour from the start, fixed rate insulin at 0.1 units per kg per hour (0.05 if glucose falls despite dextrose), stop the drug, Yellow Card, and discuss restart with the diabetes team. Glycosuria can persist for days.
  • Perioperatively in the UK: omit SGLT2 inhibitors the day before and the day of the procedure, avoid prolonged fasting, restart when eating and drinking (inpatients: consider capillary ketones below 0.6 mmol per litre). Guidance differs internationally and ketoacidosis has been reported even after more than 72 hours off the drug.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe hypercalcaemia, hypophosphataemia and refeeding syndrome
item.description:
Severe hypercalcaemia, ICU hypophosphataemia and refeeding syndrome. Hypercalcaemic crisis per the Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance (Walsh, Gittoes, Selby, 2016): thresholds, causes, 0.9% saline 4 to 6 L in 24 hours, bisphosphonates, second-line options and dialysis. The 2023 Endocrine Society guideline conditionally favours denosumab over IV bisphosphonate in malignant hypercalcaemia on low-certainty evidence; its systematic review found no significant difference in resolution, a single-arm denosumab study (33 patients, bisphosphonate-refractory) and a 2026 observational cohort (836 patients, 55 on denosumab) are the main supports, and calcitonin added nothing in the review. ICU hypophosphataemia is common and associated with mortality (Queensland cohort, 68,699 patients) and with weaning and ventilator-free-day outcomes in observational data only; a small randomised trial found enteral phosphate non-inferior to IV on biochemistry. NICE CG32 risk criteria (predictive) versus ASPEN 2020 consensus definition (diagnostic, falls of 10 to 30 percent or more within five days). The Refeeding Syndrome Trial (Doig, Lancet Respir Med 2015, 339 patients): protocolised caloric restriction did not significantly change the primary outcome (days alive after ICU discharge 44.8 vs 39.9, difference 4.9, 95% CI -2.3 to 13.6) but 60-day survival was 91 percent vs 78 percent, a secondary result to treat as hypothesis-generating.

Take-home points

  • Severe hypercalcaemia: cautious saline, then an IV antiresorptive; calcium nadirs at two to four days. Loop diuretics are not a calcium-lowering treatment.
  • Denosumab has its best data in bisphosphonate-refractory malignant hypercalcaemia; its superiority as first line is not proven, and calcitonin added no benefit in the Endocrine Society review.
  • ICU hypophosphataemia marks risk and links to worse weaning, but no trial shows that correcting it improves outcomes; replace early, enterally if the gut works, and watch renal replacement therapy.
  • For refeeding, NICE predicts risk and ASPEN diagnoses after the event; give thiamine and replace phosphate, potassium and magnesium.
  • The Refeeding Syndrome Trial was negative on its primary outcome; the survival difference was secondary, so treat caloric restriction as a reasonable option rather than proven.

item.title: Deep dive: Tumour lysis syndrome
item.description:
Tumour lysis syndrome for UK ICU: the Cairo-Bishop laboratory and clinical definitions (2004) and the 2010 expert-panel risk consensus; the BSH guidelines (Jones 2015, updated Chan 2025) as quoted in the September 2025 NHS England national patient safety alert on delayed rasburicase (123 incident reports) and in a March 2026 Oxford implementation guideline; hydration and the absence of randomised fluid data; rasburicase versus allopurinol (Cortes, J Clin Oncol 2010, 275 adults, uric acid response 87% versus 66%; surrogate endpoint, with no adult evidence of clinical benefit in a 2013 systematic review and an unclear benefit in the 2017 Cochrane review in children); fixed 3 mg prophylaxis dosing and febuxostat (FLORENCE 2015); G6PD and giving rasburicase without the result in very unwell patients; hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia and symptom-only treatment of hypocalcaemia; local renal replacement triggers and the lack of TLS-specific modality trials; spontaneous TLS (case-report level evidence); and newer agents, namely venetoclax (Roberts, NEJM 2016; MURANO 2018) and BCMA CAR-T (single-centre retrospective series). The full text of both BSH guidelines could not be opened, and the Cairo-Bishop thresholds were checked against UK local guidelines rather than the paper. No ongoing TLS trials were verified.

Take-home points

  • Risk depends on the regimen as well as the diagnosis: venetoclax can make traditionally low-risk disease high risk, and CAR-T TLS appears days after infusion alongside cytokine release syndrome.
  • High risk means hydration plus early rasburicase. Check G6PD, but BSH (as quoted in the safety alert) allows the responsible consultant to give rasburicase before the result in a very unwell patient; document the decision.
  • Rasburicase clearly lowers urate faster than allopurinol, but adult evidence of clinical benefit is lacking; fixed 3 mg prophylaxis is supported by observational data, not a randomised comparison.
  • Monitor about six-hourly and use the whole picture. In one UK local guideline, renal replacement triggers include potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more at four hours despite treatment, rising urea, creatinine or phosphate, acidosis, uraemic neurotoxicity and diuretic-resistant overload. Phosphate is hard to control without dialysis.
  • Do not treat asymptomatic hypocalcaemia and do not add potassium to fluids. Check where rasburicase is stored and how it is prescribed on your unit, as the national alert identified stock and prescribing failures.

item.title: Deep dive: Paracetamol overdose and toxic liver injury
item.description:
Paracetamol overdose and toxic liver injury for UK ICU: NAPQI and glutathione depletion as the rationale for acetylcysteine; thin randomised efficacy evidence (Cochrane 2018, eleven trials, about 700 participants, low certainty); the SNAP 12-hour regimen (Bateman, Lancet 2014, 222 patients, fewer adverse reactions, not powered for efficacy) and observational effectiveness data (Pettie 2019, 3,340 patients) plus a 2025 Edinburgh secondary analysis; RCEM 2023 default-standard statement; the 2012 MHRA/CHM single treatment line change; fomepizole and extracorporeal removal as low-evidence adjuncts for high-risk ingestions (2023 North American consensus); the HiSNAP dose trial (protocol, BMJ Open 2025); King's College criteria versus MELD (McPhail 2016 meta-analysis); non-paracetamol ALF and DILI (Cochrane 2020, EASL 2017 and 2019); and capacity, advance decisions, Mental Health Act section 63 and case law after overdose (King's College Hospital v C 2015; NHS Foundation Hospital v P 2014; B v Croydon 1995). No 2024-25 MHRA update on staggered or high-risk ingestions was found.

Take-home points

  • Use the SNAP 12-hour regimen unless toxicology advises otherwise, and know your local pathway for staggered ingestions and high-risk cases via TOXBASE and NPIS.
  • Be honest that the efficacy evidence for acetylcysteine is old and thin; the modern trials mostly address adverse reactions, not liver outcomes.
  • King's College criteria are specific but not sensitive in paracetamol failure; escalate to a liver unit on clinical trajectory, not only on meeting the criteria.
  • Fomepizole, haemodialysis and higher acetylcysteine doses in massive ingestion are low-evidence and belong in a toxicologist conversation; HiSNAP is the trial to watch.
  • Refusal after overdose starts with a decision-specific capacity assessment under the Mental Capacity Act, with early legal and psychiatric input; document it.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute mesenteric ischaemia
item.description:
Acute mesenteric ischaemia (arterial embolic or thrombotic, venous, and non-occlusive) carries about 49 per cent in-hospital mortality in the prospective AMESI study, rising to about 73 per cent for non-occlusive disease. Lactate and D-dimer are unreliable (ESVS 2025 recommends against single measurements), so early CT angiography on clinical suspicion, regardless of renal function, is the key step. ESVS 2025 and WSES 2022 both favour revascularisation before resection, damage control surgery with planned second look, antibiotics, and 24/7 multidisciplinary 'intestinal stroke' pathways, but differ in the strength of their endovascular-first and lactate wording. Evidence is almost entirely observational: a 2024 meta-analysis found no clear mortality benefit of endovascular first (OR 0.79, 0.50 to 1.25, very low certainty) and an AMESI substudy suggested patient selection explains much of the apparent advantage. Intra-arterial vasodilators for non-occlusive disease rest on retrospective data and a null Japanese matched analysis. Long-term survival is poor (about 20 per cent at five years), short bowel syndrome is uncommon, and early goals-of-care discussion and palliation are legitimate when bowel loss is massive.

Take-home points

  • Suspect mesenteric ischaemia in anyone with atrial fibrillation or vasculopathy and abdominal pain, or with new organ failure or rising pressor needs on ICU.
  • Do not rely on lactate or D-dimer, normal or raised; get CT angiography early, tell the radiologist why, and do not withhold contrast for renal function.
  • Involve vascular and gastrointestinal surgery together early: revascularise before resection, use damage control, and plan the second look.
  • For non-occlusive disease, treat the shock, minimise vasopressor dose, measure intra-abdominal pressure and decompress for compartment syndrome; intra-arterial vasodilators have weak, conflicting evidence.
  • Have an early goals-of-care conversation, since long-term survival is poor and palliation can be appropriate when bowel loss is massive.

item.title: Deep dive: Abdominal compartment syndrome
item.description:
Abdominal compartment syndrome: the World Society of the Abdominal Compartment Syndrome 2013 definitions (intra-abdominal hypertension at 12 mmHg or more, graded I to IV; syndrome at sustained pressure above 20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction), correct bladder pressure technique, risk factors from the IROI cohort (491 patients, 48.9 percent with hypertension, severity over two weeks predicting 28 and 90 day mortality), the largely weak, low-quality medical management suggestions, decompressive laparotomy as a strong recommendation on grade D evidence, open abdomen management with negative pressure therapy and early closure, the single-centre 45-patient ABThera randomised trial (90-day mortality hazard ratio 0.32, secondary outcome), the ongoing COOL trial, and the lack of any dedicated UK guideline that we could confirm.

Take-home points

  • Measure bladder pressure in anyone with risk factors, and measure it the same way every time.
  • Technique: supine, end-expiration, transducer zeroed at the midaxillary line, no more than 25 mL of saline in adults.
  • The syndrome is sustained pressure above 20 mmHg plus new organ dysfunction; follow the trend, not one number.
  • Run the medical bundle quickly, but do not let it delay decompressive laparotomy if it fails; involve surgeons early.
  • Treat the open abdomen as a bridge and plan closure from day one.

item.title: Deep dive: Budd-Chiari syndrome and hepatic vascular emergencies
item.description:
Fulminant Budd-Chiari is a rare cause of acute liver failure (about twenty of over two thousand three hundred in the US ALF Study Group registry) that is diagnosed by Doppler or CT and managed with a stepwise approach: anticoagulation, angioplasty or stenting, TIPS, then transplant. Evidence is cohort-based. The bilirubin, age and INR TIPS index identifies patients unlikely to do well with TIPS alone. MPN, including JAK2 exon twelve, is the commonest underlying cause of non-cirrhotic splanchnic vein thrombosis. Acute non-cirrhotic portal vein thrombosis recanalises in about two fifths on anticoagulation. For sinusoidal obstruction syndrome after HSCT, defibrotide is the reference treatment for severe disease (historical-control phase 3) but prophylaxis failed in the HARMONY trial.   • Acute liver failure with a congested painful liver and ascites: ask early for a hepatic vein Doppler.
  • Start anticoagulation and involve the transplant centre in parallel rather than waiting for each step to fail.
  • Send the full myeloproliferative workup including JAK2 exon twelve, and do not be put off by a negative first panel.
  • Use the bilirubin, age and INR index to flag patients unlikely to do well with TIPS alone.
  • In sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, treat severe disease early with defibrotide, but not as prophylaxis.

item.title: Deep dive: Rhabdomyolysis
item.description:
Rhabdomyolysis in ICU: risk depends on cause (cardiac arrest, sepsis, compartment syndrome worst) and is stratified by the McMahon score. Evidence for fluids is very low quality but conditionally supportive; bicarbonate and mannitol are conditionally recommended against by EAST; no randomised trials exist. Electrolytes and compartment syndrome drive early danger. Hemoadsorption for myoglobin is supported only by a conflicted Delphi consensus, not outcome data.

Take-home points

  • Stratify by cause and McMahon score; cardiac arrest, sepsis and compartment syndrome are high risk.
  • Early balanced crystalloid is reasonable (conditional, very low quality evidence); titrate and avoid overload.
  • Skip routine bicarbonate and mannitol.
  • Watch potassium and compartments; do not replace calcium without a reason.
  • Hemoadsorption is unproven on patient outcomes; keep for trials or local protocols.

item.title: Deep dive: Heparin and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia
item.description:
Heparin acts as a cofactor for antithrombin; long unfractionated chains inhibit both factor Xa and thrombin while short LMWH chains are mainly anti-Xa and renally cleared. PROTECT (2011, 3764 ICU patients) found dalteparin 5000 IU daily no different from UFH 5000 IU twice daily for proximal DVT. Monitoring by aPTT and anti-Xa often disagrees; antithrombin supplementation for heparin resistance is unproven. In HIT, the 4Ts score has a very high negative predictive value when low; testing combines immunoassay and functional assay; stop all heparin and use a non-heparin anticoagulant, with argatroban started at reduced dose in multi-organ failure per the EU SmPC. DOAC evidence is observational only.

Take-home points

  • Heparin works through antithrombin; in apparent resistance check antithrombin, factor VIII, fibrinogen and anti-Xa rather than escalating the dose.
  • PROTECT showed no DVT difference between dalteparin and UFH; use UFH or anti-Xa monitoring when renal function is poor.
  • Score the 4Ts before testing; a low score effectively excludes HIT.
  • If HIT is suspected, stop all heparin and start a non-heparin anticoagulant; argatroban starts at 0.5 microgram/kg/min in multi-organ failure, aPTT 1.5 to 3 times baseline.
  • Check doses against local formulary and haematology advice.

item.title: Deep dive: Renal tubular acidosis
item.description:
Renal tubular acidosis (proximal type 2, distal type 1, hyperkalaemic type 4) is a normal anion gap acidosis that hides inside the usual ICU hyperchloraemic acidosis from saline and gut losses. The practical points are to check the drug chart, use potassium to sort the type, interpret urine pH, urine anion gap and urine osmolar gap with caution in sepsis, AKI and with unmeasured urinary anions, replace potassium before alkali, and not extrapolate BICAR-ICU or BICARICU-2 (severe acidaemia with AKI, no mortality benefit overall) to RTA. Evidence for RTA management is physiology, case series and narrative reviews.

Take-home points

  • Hyperchloraemic acidosis with unusual potassium or phosphate: review the drug chart first (ifosfamide, tenofovir, acetazolamide, topiramate, amphotericin, lithium, trimethoprim, ACE inhibitors, heparin, calcineurin inhibitors).
  • Potassium helps sort the type: low suggests proximal or distal, high suggests type 4.
  • Urine pH, urine anion gap and osmolar gap are clues, not verdicts, in sepsis, AKI, volume depletion and with unmeasured urinary anions.
  • Replace potassium before or with alkali; proximal RTA needs large alkali doses, so in ICU treat the cause rather than chase a normal bicarbonate (expert opinion).
  • Bicarbonate trials (BICAR-ICU, BICARICU-2) were in severe acidaemia, not RTA; no outcome trial exists for hyperchloraemic acidosis.

item.title: Deep dive: Pathophysiology: Hepatorenal syndrome and the cirrhotic circulation
item.description:
Pathophysiology-led deep dive on hepatorenal syndrome: splanchnic vasodilatation (nitric oxide, bacterial translocation), effective arterial underfilling, RAAS/sympathetic/ADH activation, renal vasoconstriction with rightward-shifted autoregulation (per Deranged Physiology), and cirrhotic cardiomyopathy. Covers the move from type 1/2 to HRS-AKI/AKD/CKD (2024 ICA-ADQI consensus), then maps mechanism to treatment: terlipressin plus albumin (CONFIRM, with the respiratory failure signal), noradrenaline as an alternative (small open-label trials, 2024 meta-analysis), and transplant as definitive with RRT as a bridge.

Take-home points

  • HRS-AKI is a circulatory (functional) problem: exclude fluid responsiveness, nephrotoxins and infection, then vasoconstrictor plus albumin.
  • CONFIRM: verified reversal 32% vs 17% (terlipressin vs placebo); no survival benefit shown; respiratory-disorder death within 90 days 11% vs 2%.
  • If using terlipressin, check for volume overload and severe ACLF and monitor oxygenation.
  • Noradrenaline is a credible alternative on low-certainty evidence (meta-analysis RR for response 1.19, 0.96 to 1.46).
  • RRT replaces filtration, not the circulation: bridge only; raise transplant candidacy early.

item.title: Deep dive: Upper GI and variceal haemorrhage
item.description:
Deep dive for a UK ICU consultant on upper GI and variceal haemorrhage. Covers the portal-pressure rationale, restrictive transfusion (Villanueva 2013, TRIGGER 2015), tranexamic acid (HALT-IT 2020, negative with more venous thromboembolism), vasoactive drugs, antibiotics (Fernandez 2006), pre-emptive TIPS (Garcia-Pagan 2010, Lv 2019, IPD meta-analysis 2024 versus a 2026 RCT-only meta-analysis), endoscopy timing (Lau 2020; 24 hours in BSG/NICE versus 12 hours in Baveno VII), Glasgow-Blatchford, pre-endoscopy PPIs, airway protection, erythromycin, balloon tamponade versus stents, and where BSG 2015, NICE CG141 and Baveno VII differ.

Take-home points

  • Restrictive transfusion (about 70 to 80 g/L) in haemodynamically stable variceal bleeders; benefit in Villanueva was seen in Child-Pugh A/B, not C.
  • Do not give tranexamic acid for GI bleeding (HALT-IT: no mortality benefit, more venous thromboembolism).
  • Vasoactive drug and antibiotic from admission; ceftriaxone favoured in advanced cirrhosis or high quinolone resistance.
  • Identify Child-Pugh C (under 14) or B with active bleeding early and contact the TIPS centre; Baveno VII says pre-emptive TIPS within 72 hours, ideally under 24.
  • Intubate before endoscopy if vomiting blood or reduced consciousness, extubate early; stent or balloon is a bridge to TIPS.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe acute pancreatitis
item.description:
Severe acute pancreatitis is defined by persistent organ failure beyond forty-eight hours (revised Atlanta 2013). Recent trials shifted practice towards moderate, goal-directed lactated Ringer's (WATERFALL), feeding as tolerated without needing early tube feeding (PYTHON), no routine antibiotic prophylaxis (Cochrane), and for infected necrosis a step-up approach with postponed drainage (PANTER, TENSION, POINTER). Abdominal compartment syndrome follows WSACS 2013 consensus.

Take-home points

  • Moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer's, reassess often; aggressive hydration caused more fluid overload without benefit in WATERFALL.
  • Feed early as tolerated; oral if possible, tube if not; no routine prophylactic antibiotics.
  • Measure bladder pressure when the abdomen is tense and organ failure is rising.
  • Infected necrosis: antibiotics first, postpone drainage if stable, then step up; endoscopic and surgical step-up gave similar primary outcomes.

item.title: Deep dive: Major haemorrhage in trauma
item.description:
Deep dive on major haemorrhage in trauma for a UK ICU consultant audience. It opens with the pathophysiology of acute traumatic coagulopathy, then walks the randomised evidence: tranexamic acid (CRASH-2 positive, PATCH-Trauma neutral on its primary outcome), component ratios (PROPPR, no significant mortality difference), prehospital blood (RePHILL neutral; SWiFT and TOWAR whole blood trials neutral), empirical early cryoprecipitate (CRYOSTAT-2 neutral), viscoelastic-guided protocols (ITACTIC neutral), permissive hypotension (older and pilot data), calcium (observational only, CAVALIER ongoing) and REBOA (UK-REBOA: no reduction in, and possibly increased, mortality). Guidelines compared are NICE NG39 (2016) and the European guideline (sixth edition, 2023). Ends with five Monday take-homes.

Take-home points

  • Give tranexamic acid early and within three hours of injury (one gram, then one gram over eight hours); CRASH-2 benefit was time-dependent, and PATCH-Trauma was neutral on functional outcome with secondary mortality signals only.
  • Higher plasma and platelet ratios are reasonable, but PROPPR showed no significant 24-hour or 30-day mortality difference, only less death from exsanguination and more haemostasis.
  • Prehospital whole blood (SWiFT, TOWAR) and empirical early cryoprecipitate (CRYOSTAT-2) have not been shown to beat standard care; use them if available, but do not delay standard resuscitation.
  • Monitor and correct ionised calcium (European guideline grade 1C), recognising the evidence is observational and prehospital calcium trials are still running.
  • Be cautious with REBOA: in UK-REBOA it did not reduce, and may have increased, 90-day mortality.

item.title: Deep dive: Obstetric critical care: postpartum haemorrhage and pre-eclampsia
item.description:
Deep dive on obstetric critical care. Pregnancy is hypercoagulable with high term fibrinogen, so bleeding is under-recognised and fibrinogen replacement is not a reflex. Early tranexamic acid treatment reduces bleeding death (WOMAN); prophylaxis is mixed (TRAAP, TRAAP2, WOMAN-2, 2024 IPD meta-analysis). The E-MOTIVE detection-plus-bundle approach cut a severe-PPH composite in vaginal births in four African countries. Fibrinogen concentrate trials (FIB-PPH, OBS2) were neutral; OBS-UK is unreported as far as we could find. Magnesium sulphate halves eclampsia (Magpie); BP-target trials (CHIPS, CHAP) are in milder disease; fluid restriction evidence is a single 46-woman pilot. Brief UKOSS data on amniotic fluid embolism and sepsis, and system-level guidance.

Take-home points

  • Give tranexamic acid early (ideally within 3 hours) to any woman with PPH, without waiting for labs.
  • Measure blood loss objectively and use a timely first-response bundle (E-MOTIVE lesson).
  • Do not give plasma or fibrinogen by reflex; check fibrinogen or use viscoelastic testing and treat low values.
  • Magnesium sulphate for severe pre-eclampsia; be humble about fluid and BP targets as the evidence is thin.
  • Peripartum sepsis (especially group A strep) progresses fast; give antibiotics early.

item.title: Deep dive: ECMO in adult critical care: VV and VA
item.description:
Deep dive for a UK ICU consultant in a non-ECMO centre. VV-ECMO: CESAR (referral to an ECMO centre improved survival without severe disability), EOLIA (neutral on 60-day mortality, high crossover) and the post hoc Bayesian re-analysis (probably modest benefit); NHS England adult respiratory ECMO service specification (2019 version read) for referral criteria. VA-ECMO: ECLS-SHOCK neutral with more bleeding and vascular complications; pooled RCTs consistent. ECPR: ARREST (small, positive), Prague OHCA and INCEPTION (neutral on primary).   • ECPR is a system question with short low-flow times; RCTs (Prague, INCEPTION) were neutral on primary outcomes.

item.title: Deep dive: Severe hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia
item.description:
Severe hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia, covered for a UK ICU consultant audience. Hyponatraemia: SALSA (open-label RCT, 178 patients) found no significant difference in overcorrection between bolus and slow infusion of 3% saline but less need for re-lowering with boluses (secondary outcome). Large observational cohorts and a 2025 meta-analysis question very slow correction and show ODS to be rare, with risk factors (alcohol, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia) perhaps mattering more than rate; all are confounded. Rescue with desmopressin plus or minus dextrose rests on a small retrospective series. Hyperkalaemia: the UK Kidney Association 2023 guideline (read in its public-consultation draft form) sets a five-step approach: calcium, 10 units insulin with 25 g glucose plus a 10% glucose infusion if pre-treatment glucose is below 7, adjunct salbutamol, no routine bicarbonate, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for emergency use, and early renal or critical care decisions on RRT. Evidence for binders in the acute setting is thin (HARMONIZE was outpatient; PLATINUM was negative and underpowered).

Take-home points

  • Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia: hypertonic saline boluses, small rapid rise, then stop and recheck. SALSA: overcorrection 17.2% vs 24.2% (not significant); re-lowering 41.4% vs 57.1% (secondary).
  • Identify ODS risk (alcohol, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, hypophosphataemia), expect water diuresis, and have desmopressin plus or minus dextrose ready as rescue (evidence is retrospective and small).
  • Observational data suggest very slow correction in low-risk patients is not clearly safer; no randomised trial of correction limits exists.
  • Hyperkalaemia: calcium for ECG changes; insulin-glucose with a 10% glucose follow-on if glucose is below 7 mmol/l; monitor glucose for six hours; salbutamol only as an adjunct.
  • No routine IV bicarbonate; involve renal or critical care early when oliguric or resistant, and consider SZC in severe hyperkalaemia.

item.title: Deep dive: Guillain-Barre syndrome and myasthenic crisis in the ICU
item.description:
Deep dive on Guillain-Barre syndrome (GBS) and myasthenic crisis in ICU. Covers ventilation decisions (Lawn 20/30/40 heuristic, Erasmus respiratory insufficiency score, bulbar weakness, serial spirometry), IVIG versus plasma exchange (PE/Sandoglobulin 1997, Cochrane reviews), the negative SID-GBS second-dose trial, the 2023 EAN/PNS guideline, complement and FcRn agents (briefly), and crisis outcomes. Emphasis is on what changes bedside decisions, with explicit statements where evidence could not be checked.

Take-home points

  • Trend vital capacity and respiratory pressures rather than relying on oximetry; weigh bulbar weakness, cough and rapid progression heavily and intubate electively.
  • Use the Erasmus respiratory insufficiency score at admission to identify who needs critical care.
  • IVIG and plasma exchange are equivalent in GBS; choose by logistics and haemodynamics; no second IVIG dose (SID-GBS; EAN/PNS 2023).

item.title: Deep dive: Ventilator-associated pneumonia
item.description:
Ventilator-associated pneumonia has no diagnostic gold standard, and the evidence for prevention is mostly about lowering VAP rates rather than mortality. Head-up positioning and toothbrushing are cheap, low-quality-evidence essentials. Subglottic drainage lowers VAP (Damas 2015) without clear effects on mortality or ventilation time. Chlorhexidine mouthcare shows no VAP benefit in non-cardiac surgical patients and a non-significant mortality signal, while CHORAL found no mortality change on de-adoption. SuDDICU (2022) did not show a significant hospital mortality reduction (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.02) but lowered resistant organism cultures; the earlier Dutch trial was positive and the high-resistance European trial was neutral. Single-dose ceftriaxone (PROPHY-VAP, brain injury) and inhaled amikacin (AMIKINHAL) reduce VAP incidence. For treatment, 8 days matches 15 days in the 2003 trial (with more recurrence for non-fermenters), and REGARD-VAP (2024) supports individualised short courses (median 6 days).

Take-home points

  • Head of bed 30 to 45 degrees and daily toothbrushing (without chlorhexidine) are the low-cost essentials; the evidence quality is low to moderate.
  • Take a lower respiratory sample before antibiotics where possible and use it to narrow therapy; neither BAL with quantitative culture nor aspirate with plain culture changed 28-day mortality in the Canadian trial.
  • For responders, aim for 7 days or fewer; REGARD-VAP showed non-inferiority of individualised short course (median 6 days vs 14).
  • SDD is a unit-level decision that depends on baseline resistance; SuDDICU was not significant for mortality, and the benefit in acute brain injury is post hoc.
  • In acute brain injury consider single-dose ceftriaxone (PROPHY-VAP); inhaled amikacin lowers VAP but mortality benefit is unproven.
  • Chlorhexidine: not proven to harm, no clear benefit in non-cardiac surgical patients.

item.title: Deep dive: ICU-acquired weakness
item.description:
ICU-acquired weakness (critical illness polyneuropathy and myopathy) is common in long-stay patients and is associated with slower weaning and higher one-year mortality in matched cohort data. Plausible mechanisms (unloading, catabolism, hyperglycaemia, sepsis, steroids) have not translated into reliable interventions: tight glycaemic control reduced CIP/CIM in early single-centre trials but increased mortality in NICE-SUGAR; TEAM found no benefit from higher-dose early mobilisation and more adverse events; EFFORT Protein found no benefit from high-dose protein, with possible harm in AKI and high organ failure subgroups. Practical advice: moderate glucose control, safe usual-plus mobilisation, no routine high protein push, and strength testing once the patient is awake.

Take-home points

  • TEAM (NEJM 2022): more mobilisation was not better; do usual-plus mobilisation safely.
  • Avoid tight glucose targets despite the early CIP/CIM signal; NICE-SUGAR showed excess mortality and severe hypoglycaemia.
  • Do not default to high-dose protein, especially in AKI or high organ failure scores (EFFORT Protein, subgroup signal only).
  • Assess strength (MRC sum score) once awake; persistent weakness at ICU discharge carries worse prognosis.
  • Be honest with families: trial evidence here is mixed and nothing proven treats established weakness.

item.title: Deep dive: Status epilepticus in the ICU
item.description:
Benzodiazepine resistance grows with seizure duration (GABA-A receptor internalisation, preclinical mechanism), so early adequate first-line treatment matters (RAMPART: IM midazolam 73.4% vs IV lorazepam 63.4% seizure-free on arrival). For benzodiazepine-refractory convulsive SE, ESETT found levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate equivalent (47%, 45%, 46% at 60 min); paediatric EcLiPSE and ConSEPT showed no significant difference between levetiracetam and phenytoin. Anaesthetic choice (midazolam, propofol, barbiturate), ketamine in super-refractory SE and EEG targets rest on observational data and consensus. CERTA showed continuous EEG detected more seizures but did not change 6-month mortality versus routine EEG. Mortality about 10% responsive, 25% refractory, nearly 40% super-refractory (ICM review).

Take-home points

  • Treat early and adequately; benzodiazepine efficacy falls with time. Do not wait for IV access (IM midazolam).
  • Second-line drug choice is practical (levetiracetam, valproate, phenytoin/fosphenytoin): about half respond to any of them.
  • Do not dither over a third non-sedating drug; plan anaesthesia with airway and vasopressor ready (consensus).
  • Get EEG and look for the cause (autoimmune, infective).
  • Ketamine, anaesthetic agent and EEG depth targets are consensus/observational; say so.

item.title: Deep dive: DKA and HHS in the ICU
item.description:
Fluid choice is the one area with trial data. SCOPE-DKA (phase 2, 90 patients) was negative on its 48 hour primary outcome; the 24 hour benefit for Plasma-Lyte was secondary. The SMART/SALT-ED DKA subgroup (172 adults, post hoc) found faster resolution with balanced fluid (13.0 vs 16.9 hours). BEST-DKA (phase 3, protocol only) is awaited. The 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus and the JBDS DKA guideline (revised March 2023) agree on fixed-rate insulin 0.1 units/kg/h, reducing to 0.05 with dextrose once glucose is below about 14 mmol/L (expert consensus; a 2025 five-hospital UK audit showed patchy uptake and no demonstrable outcome change). Bicarbonate is not routine (consensus allows pH below 7.0). HHS needs slower correction (osmolality fall 3.0 to 8.0 mOsm/kg/h), FRIII at 0.05 units/kg/h once osmolality stops falling, and prophylactic LMWH. SGLT2 inhibitor DKA can be euglycaemic: MHRA (2020) advises interrupting treatment during major surgery or serious illness and checking blood ketones; the 2025 Anaesthesia Delphi consensus advises omitting them the day before and day of elective procedures.

Take-home points

  • Low pH with normal glucose in anyone on an SGLT2 inhibitor is DKA until proven otherwise: check blood ketones, start dextrose with insulin.
  • Balanced crystalloid is reasonable in ICU (JBDS accepts it), but the benefit shown is faster biochemical resolution, not proven patient-centred outcomes.
  • Replace potassium early; consensus holds insulin if potassium is below 3.5 mmol/L on arrival.
  • No routine bicarbonate; consensus allows it at pH below 7.0, JBDS notes occasional ICU use with inotropes (pragmatic, not trial-based).
  • HHS: go slow, monitor osmolality, give prophylactic LMWH; watch for mixed DKA/HHS, which had the highest mortality in the cited cohort.

item.title: Deep dive: Acute liver failure and acute-on-chronic liver failure
item.description:
Hyperacute/acute liver failure (mostly paracetamol in the UK) is managed around cerebral oedema (ammonia-driven astrocyte swelling), supportive organ care, no routine INR correction, and early transplant-centre contact using the UK revised criteria (successor to King's College). Evidence for ammonia-lowering CRRT is physiological and consensus-based, hypertonic saline has a small RCT, prophylactic hypothermia failed, and high-volume plasma exchange improved transplant-free hospital survival in one open-label RCT. ACLF (EASL-CLIF) is graded by organ-failure count with 28-day mortality of roughly 20, 30 and 80 percent for grades 1 to 3. EASL 2023 advises reassessing at 3 to 7 days and considering withdrawal if 4 or more organ failures or CLIF-C ACLF over 70 with no salvage transplant option (level 4, consensus). APACHE (reported June 2026, conference only, sponsor-funded, open-label, stopped at 274 of 380) suggests plasma exchange with albumin lowers 90-day death before transplant, but combined death-or-transplant was similar; the 2023 guideline pre-dates it and does not recommend plasma exchange outside trials.

Take-home points

  • Hyperacute ALF: head up, avoid hyponatraemia, sodium 145 to 155 with hypertonic saline if at risk, no prophylactic cooling, consider CRRT to keep ammonia under 100 (consensus, not outcome-proven), do not correct INR unless bleeding or high-risk procedure.
  • Call the liver centre early; use the current UK revised criteria, not memory of the original King's criteria. Criteria identify who dies without a graft, not who tolerates one.
  • ACLF: count organ failures, score sequentially, make prognostic and futility judgements after 3 to 7 days of full support, not on day one.
  • Document ceilings of care as conditional (no transplant option, named criteria, named time point). EASL futility criteria are level 4 consensus: "consider", not "mandate".
  • Plasma exchange in ACLF: promising (APACHE) but unpublished in full; wait for the paper and local policy.

item.title: Deep dive: Strong ion difference and the Stewart approach to acid-base
item.description:
Stewart's physicochemical approach to acid-base: the three independent variables (strong ion difference, total weak acids, pCO2), apparent versus effective SID and the strong ion gap, and how this compares with Henderson-Hasselbalch, the albumin-corrected anion gap and Fencl-Story / partitioned base excess. Includes a worked example in which low albumin hides an unmeasured-anion acidosis, why saline (SID zero) and balanced crystalloids (effective SID about 28) pull plasma in different directions, and an honest look at what SMART, SPLIT, BaSICS and PLUS show.

Take-home points

  • Stewart's independent variables are SID, total weak acid (mainly albumin and phosphate) and pCO2; hydrogen ion and bicarbonate are dependent, not causal.
  • The approach is mathematically consistent with the traditional one; its practical value is forcing you to read chloride, sodium and albumin together.
  • Always correct the anion gap for albumin: a normal gap with albumin of 20 g/L may hide unmeasured anions.
  • Saline (SID 0) and balanced crystalloids (effective SID about 28) pull plasma SID toward the fluid's own; that is real chemistry.
  • SMART showed a small kidney-event benefit; BaSICS and PLUS showed no mortality difference. Prefer balanced fluids in volume, take care in brain injury (BaSICS subgroup signal), and don't act on a chloride number alone.

item.title: Deep dive: The revised Starling equation and the glycocalyx
item.description:
The classic Starling picture (filtration at the arterial end, reabsorption at the venous end) against the revised model of Levick and Michel and Woodcock: the glycocalyx and subglycocalyx space set the effective oncotic gradient, steady-state capillaries filter throughout with no venous reabsorption, and lymph returns the filtrate. Covers what damages the glycocalyx, the status of syndecan-1 and heparan sulphate as biomarkers, and the consequences for albumin (SAFE, ALBIOS), context sensitivity of volume effect, oedema that colloid cannot draw back, and restrictive fluids and de-resuscitation (CLASSIC, CLOVERS).

Take-home points

  • In steady state capillaries filter along their whole length; there is no sustained venous reabsorption and lymph returns the filtrate.
  • The oncotic gradient that matters is across the glycocalyx (plasma versus subglycocalyx space); interstitial oncotic pressure matters little.
  • Glycocalyx shedding is linked to sepsis, surgery, hyperglycaemia and probably hypervolaemia, but syndecan-1 and heparan sulphate are research markers, not decision tools.
  • Albumin and other colloids are less volume-sparing than predicted and will not pull oedema back.
  • Give fluid for a reason, reassess, and plan de-resuscitation early; CLASSIC and CLOVERS found no mortality difference between restrictive and liberal strategies.

item.title: Deep dive: Procalcitonin in the ICU
item.description:
Procalcitonin as a tool to stop rather than start antibiotics in ICU. Biology and kinetics, non-infective causes of a raised level (surgery, trauma, burns, pancreatitis, cardiogenic shock, renal impairment and RRT), then the trials: ProACT (no benefit in ED lower respiratory tract infection), PRORATA, SAPS and the UK ADAPT-Sepsis trial (antibiotic duration 9.8 vs 10.7 days, a difference of 0.88 days; 28-day mortality 20.9% vs 19.4%, non-inferior within a 5.4% margin; CRP-guided advice had no effect). Meta-analyses give borderline, low-certainty mortality signals. Guidelines: Surviving Sepsis 2021 (weak, low quality), NICE 2015 diagnostics guidance now being updated, and the COVID-19 experience. Ends with a practical ICU stopping approach.

Take-home points

  • In ICU, think of procalcitonin as a stopping aid, not a starting test.
  • ADAPT-Sepsis: under one day shorter antibiotic courses, non-inferior mortality within the margin but a point estimate 1.5 percentage points higher; CRP-guided advice made no difference.
  • Use the trend, check for non-infective causes, and never stop against the clinical picture or where a fixed course is needed (S. aureus bacteraemia, endocarditis, undrained collections).
  • NICE is updating its procalcitonin guidance; watch for it.
